chapters.name: Chapter 1: Climate risk is a business risk

lessons.title: Lesson 1: A climate-risk assessment for your farm business
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Rate the climate risks to your farm business by likelihood and money impact.
This lesson builds toward: Given your farm's enterprises and what happened in the last five seasons, you will rate the main climate risks to your farm business by how likely they are and how much money they could cost, listing at least three risks, each with an estimated cost in local currency.
A climate-risk calendar shows when weather hurts your farm. A climate-risk assessment goes one step further: it asks how much each risk could cost your business, so you know which ones to spend money on first.
For each enterprise (maize, tomatoes, goats, cocoa, tilapia), list the climate hazards: a late start to the rains, a dry spell at flowering, heat stress in animals, floods, strong winds, new pests. Ask two questions about each: How likely is it in the next five seasons (low, medium or high)? And if it happens, how much income would you lose? Use your records and ask older farmers what happened in past bad years.
Then think about the whole business, not only the field: Can you still repay a loan in a bad year? Will buyers still take your produce if quality drops? Can workers reach the farm in floods? A dry spell that cuts 40 bags of maize to 25 is not only a yield problem; it is a cash-flow problem.
Put the risks in a simple table and rank them. The risks that are both likely and costly go to the top of your plan.
Step by step:
- List your enterprises.
- Under each, list climate hazards from your experience and your risk calendar.
- Mark each hazard's likelihood: low, medium or high.
- Estimate the money lost if it happens, in your currency.
- Rank: likely and costly risks first.
- Add business effects: loan repayment, buyer contracts, labour, transport.
Words to know:
- Climate-risk assessment: a list of the climate hazards your business faces, how likely each is and how much it could cost.
- Hazard: an event that can cause harm, such as drought, flood or heat.
- Likelihood: how probable it is that something will happen.
- Impact: how much damage or money loss an event causes.
Official sources:
- FAO: Climate-Smart Agriculture Sourcebook
Try it now: Make a table with four columns: hazard, likelihood (low, medium, high), estimated money lost, and business effect. Fill in at least three hazards for your own farm and circle the top one.
You can now rate the climate risks to your farm business by how likely they are and how much they could cost.

check.q: Which risk belongs at the top of a farm's climate-risk plan?
options: One that is unlikely and cheap
One that is likely and would cost a lot
One that only affects the neighbour
One that happened once 40 years ago
check.why: Risks that are both likely and costly do the most harm to the business, so they come first.

check.q: A dry spell cuts a farmer's maize harvest and she cannot repay her loan on time. What does this show?
options: Climate risk only affects yields
Loans are never affected by weather
Climate risk also hits cash flow and repayments
The farmer should stop keeping records
check.why: A climate-risk assessment looks at the whole business, including cash flow and debts.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Choosing and costing adaptation investments
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Cost two adaptation investments and compare their payback.
This lesson builds toward: Given two or three possible adaptation investments, you will cost each investment and compare its yearly benefit with its cost, using your own local prices and showing the payback in seasons or years.
An adaptation investment is money or work you spend now to lose less in bad years. Common ones in Africa are drought-tolerant or early-maturing seed (CGIAR centres such as CIMMYT have bred drought-tolerant maize), water storage (tanks, lined ponds), shade trees for cocoa, coffee or animals, better animal housing, and diversification: adding a second crop, goats, poultry or fish so one bad season does not ruin you.
For each option, write the cost (buying, building, labour, upkeep) and the yearly benefit (extra harvest in a bad year, less feed bought, a new income). Then work out the payback: cost divided by yearly benefit gives roughly how many years until it pays for itself. Remember that some benefits only come in bad years, so average them over several seasons.
Example with made-up figures: a farmer in Machakos compares a water tank at KES 60,000 that saves about KES 20,000 a year in bought water and lost vegetables (payback about 3 years), with drought-tolerant seed that costs KES 2,000 more per acre and saves about KES 8,000 in a dry year that comes one year in two (average KES 4,000 a year, payback in the first season). Both may be worth doing; the seed is cheaper to start.
Also check: Can you maintain it? Does it fit your labour and land? Does it work in a good year too? Ask your extension officer which varieties and designs suit your area.
Step by step:
- Pick your top risk from Lesson 1.
- List two or three investments that reduce it.
- Write each one's full cost: buy, build, labour, upkeep.
- Estimate the yearly benefit, averaged over good and bad years.
- Payback = cost ÷ yearly benefit.
- Check labour, upkeep and fit with extension advice.
Words to know:
- Adaptation investment: money or work spent now so you lose less when the climate hits.
- Payback: how long it takes for the money an investment saves or earns to cover its cost.
- Diversification: having more than one source of income so one failure does not ruin the business.
Official sources:
- CGIAR: Climate-smart (drought-tolerant) maize
- FAO: Climate-Smart Agriculture Sourcebook
Try it now: For your top risk, cost two adaptation investments with your own local prices. Write the cost, the average yearly benefit and the payback for each, then circle the one you would start with and say why.
You can now cost adaptation investments and compare them by their payback.

check.q: A shade-net costs GHS 3,000 and saves about GHS 1,000 a year in lost tomatoes. What is the rough payback?
options: 3 months
1 year
10 years
About 3 years
check.why: Payback is cost divided by yearly benefit: 3,000 ÷ 1,000 = about 3 years (example figures).

check.q: Drought-tolerant seed only helps in dry years, which come about one year in three. How should you count its benefit?
options: Average the dry-year saving over all the years
Count the dry-year saving every year
Count no benefit at all
Only count it in wet years
check.why: Benefits that come only in bad years should be averaged over good and bad years.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Climate finance and green loans
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List the questions to ask before taking a climate or green loan and check the lender is licensed.
This lesson builds toward: Before you apply for a climate or green loan, grant or programme, you will list the questions to ask the lender and check that it is licensed, covering the total cost, repayment dates, conditions and who regulates it.
Climate finance is money meant for adapting to climate change or cutting emissions. Large funds such as the Green Climate Fund do not lend to farmers directly; they work through governments, banks and agencies. What reaches farmers usually comes as: green or climate loans from banks, microfinance banks and SACCOs (for tanks, solar pumps, drip kits, biogas); pay-as-you-go plans from equipment suppliers; programmes by the government or NGOs that share the cost of seed, tanks or trees; and grants or matching funds for groups and cooperatives.
Where to ask: your bank or SACCO, your cooperative, your county or state agriculture office and extension officer, and agricultural banks such as the Bank of Agriculture in Nigeria or the Agricultural Development Bank in Ghana. Programmes change often, so ask what is open now and get the details in writing.
A green label does not make a loan cheap or safe. Compare the total cost (interest, fees, insurance), when repayments fall (do they match your harvest?), what happens if the harvest fails, and any conditions (approved suppliers, training, insurance). Check the lender is licensed: in Kenya on the Central Bank of Kenya lists, in Nigeria with the Central Bank of Nigeria, elsewhere with your central bank or cooperative regulator.
Never pay a "processing fee" to an agent to get a grant or loan, and never share your PIN or mobile money code.
Step by step:
- Decide what the money will buy and its payback (Lesson 2).
- Ask your bank, SACCO, cooperative and agriculture office what is open now.
- Get the total cost, repayment dates and conditions in writing.
- Check the lender on the central bank or regulator's list.
- Ask: what happens if my harvest fails?
- Talk to a trusted adviser before you sign.
Words to know:
- Climate finance: money for adapting to climate change or cutting emissions.
- Green loan: a loan for something that helps the environment, such as a solar pump or biogas unit.
- SACCO: a savings and credit cooperative owned by its members.
- Pay-as-you-go: paying for equipment in small regular amounts, often by mobile money.
Official sources:
- Green Climate Fund (works through governments, banks and accredited agencies, not directly with farmers)
- Central Bank of Kenya (lists of licensed banks and microfinance banks)
- Central Bank of Nigeria (licensed institutions and consumer protection)
- Bank of Agriculture, Nigeria
- Agricultural Development Bank, Ghana
Try it now: Write five questions you will ask a lender or programme about the investment you chose in Lesson 2. Include total cost, repayment dates, conditions, what happens if the harvest fails, and how you will check they are licensed.
You can now list the questions to ask about a climate or green loan and check that the lender is licensed.

check.q: An agent says you will get a climate grant if you first send KES 3,000 as a processing fee. What should you do?
options: Pay quickly before the grant closes
Send half now and half later
Refuse; real programmes do not ask agents to collect fees like this
Give the agent your mobile money PIN instead
check.why: Upfront "processing fees" to agents are a common scam; check the programme with the official office.

check.q: Which question matters most when comparing two green loans for a solar pump?
options: Which one has the nicest logo
The total cost and whether repayments match your harvest
Which agent is friendliest
Which one is called green
check.why: Total cost and repayment timing decide whether you can afford the loan, whatever its label.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Cutting costs, carbon and planning

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Mitigation that also saves money
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Identify two practices on your farm that cut emissions and costs at the same time.
This lesson builds toward: Given the practices you use now, you will identify two practices that cut greenhouse gas emissions and also cut your costs, naming the input or money each one saves.
Mitigation means cutting the greenhouse gases a farm releases, or storing more carbon in soil and trees. For a farmer, the best mitigation is the kind that also saves money, because you gain even if no one pays you for the carbon.
Less fertilizer waste: fertilizer lost to rain, wind or the wrong timing is money lost and also releases gases. Placing it near the roots at the right time, and adding manure and compost, gets more harvest from each bag. Biogas: a household biodigester turns cow or pig dung into cooking gas, cutting what you spend on firewood or charcoal, and the leftover bio-slurry is a fertilizer. The Africa Biogas Partnership Programme has helped install household biodigesters in Kenya, Burkina Faso and other countries.
Agroforestry: trees on the farm store carbon and can give fruit, fodder, firewood, timber and shade (for example shade trees in cocoa in Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana), cutting what you buy. Other savers: not burning crop residues (keeps nutrients and saves fertilizer), better feed for animals (more milk per animal), and solar pumps instead of diesel (lower running cost).
Write the saving in money. If a biodigester costs XOF 500,000 and saves XOF 120,000 a year in charcoal and fertilizer (made-up figures), you can work out its payback like any other investment.
Step by step:
- List the inputs you buy most: fertilizer, fuel, feed, firewood.
- For each, find a practice that uses less or replaces it.
- Estimate the money saved per year.
- Check the cost and payback.
- Pick two to start.
Words to know:
- Mitigation: cutting greenhouse gas emissions, or storing more carbon in soil and trees.
- Biodigester: a sealed tank where dung breaks down and makes biogas for cooking or light.
- Bio-slurry: the liquid left after biogas is made; it can be used as fertilizer.
- Agroforestry: growing trees together with crops or animals on the same land.
Official sources:
- SNV/Hivos: Africa Biogas Partnership Programme factsheet (household biodigesters and bio-slurry)
- FAO: Agroforestry
- FAO: Climate-Smart Agriculture Sourcebook
Try it now: List the three inputs you spend most on. For each, write one practice that would use less of it, and estimate the money saved per year. Choose two to put in your plan.
You can now identify practices that cut both emissions and costs, and put the saving in money.

check.q: Which practice cuts emissions and also saves a pig farmer money?
options: Burning dung in the open
Buying more charcoal
Leaving dung in a heap by the river
A biodigester that makes cooking gas and bio-slurry fertilizer
check.why: Biogas replaces bought fuel and the bio-slurry replaces some fertilizer.

check.q: Why is reducing fertilizer waste a good mitigation choice for a farmer?
options: It saves money as well as cutting emissions
It makes the soil harder
It means you never need to fertilize again
It is required by every buyer
check.why: Less waste means more harvest per bag, so the farmer saves money and emits less.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Carbon credits: chances, scams and unfair contracts
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Check a carbon credit offer for warning signs before you sign or pay anything.
This lesson builds toward: Given a carbon credit offer or contract, you will check the offer for the warning signs of a scam or an unfair deal, answering at least four checks before you sign or pay anything.
A carbon credit is a certificate that says one tonne of carbon dioxide was kept out of the air or stored, for example by planting trees, restoring land or using clean cookstoves. Companies buy credits. Some projects pay farmers or communities for practices that store carbon. Real projects are registered with a standard such as Verra or Gold Standard, and their registries can be searched by project name.
Be very careful. Carbon payments are often small, slow (sometimes years after you start) and uncertain, and costs for measuring and checking are taken first. Scams and unfair deals are common: people who ask farmers for a fee to "join", promise big quick payments, or ask you to sign long contracts that give away rights to your land, trees or carbon for 20 years or more.
Warning signs: you must pay to join; big payments are promised fast; you cannot take the contract away to read; it is not in a language you understand; it gives someone rights over your land or trees, or stops you cutting or selling them; it does not say how much you get, when, and what share goes to the developer; the project is not on any registry.
Some countries now have rules. Kenya's Climate Change (Carbon Markets) Regulations, 2024 require approval of carbon projects and, for projects on community land, a community development agreement on how benefits are shared. Check your own country's rules with the environment ministry. Never sign on the day; read it all, ask your cooperative, a lawyer or a trusted adviser, and keep a copy.
Step by step:
- Ask: what is the project's name and registry ID?
- Look it up on the registry (Verra, Gold Standard or others).
- Ask what you will be paid, when, and what share the developer keeps.
- Read what rights over land, trees or carbon you give, and for how long.
- Refuse any joining fee.
- Take the contract away; get advice before signing; keep a copy.
Words to know:
- Carbon credit: a certificate for one tonne of carbon dioxide kept out of the air or stored.
- Carbon project developer: the company that runs a carbon project and sells the credits.
- Registry: an official public list of carbon projects and their credits.
- Benefit sharing: how the money from credits is split between the developer, farmers and community.
Official sources:
- Verra registry (look up a carbon project by name or ID)
- Gold Standard registry (look up a carbon project by name or ID)
- Kenya: The Climate Change (Carbon Markets) Regulations, 2024 (summary and full text)
Try it now: Write a checklist of at least five questions you will ask before joining any carbon credit scheme. Then imagine an agent offers your group XOF 50,000 per farmer if you sign today and pay XOF 5,000 to register: mark which warning signs this offer shows.
You can now check a carbon credit offer for the warning signs of a scam or an unfair contract.

check.q: A carbon agent asks each farmer to pay NGN 10,000 to join and promises payment next month. What is this most likely?
options: A normal registered project
A government subsidy
A scam or very unfair offer
A free training
check.why: Joining fees and fast big promises are classic warning signs of carbon scams.

check.q: What should you look for in a carbon contract before signing?
options: How much you get, when, and what rights over land or trees you give and for how long
Only the colour of the logo
Whether the agent is friendly
Nothing, if the project is about trees
check.why: Payment, timing and rights over your land or trees decide whether the deal is fair.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Adding climate risk to your business plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a one-page climate-resilience plan for your farm business.
This lesson builds toward: Using your work from this course, you will write a one-page climate-resilience plan for your farm business, with risks, investments, costs, finance, money-saving practices and a review date. Given your farm's enterprises and what happened in the last five seasons, you will rate the main climate risks to your farm business by how likely they are and how much money they could cost, listing at least three risks, each with an estimated cost in local currency. Given two or three possible adaptation investments, you will cost each investment and compare its yearly benefit with its cost, using your own local prices and showing the payback in seasons or years.
Lenders, buyers and programmes increasingly ask how a farm will cope with climate shocks. A short climate section in your business plan shows you have thought about it, and it helps you decide where your own money goes first.
Your one-page plan has six parts: 1. your top three climate risks with their likelihood and cost (Lesson 1); 2. two or three adaptation investments with cost, benefit and payback (Lesson 2); 3. how you will pay: savings, group, loan or programme, and your questions for the lender (Lesson 3); 4. two practices that cut costs and emissions (Lesson 4); 5. your rules for any carbon offer (Lesson 5); 6. a review date after each season.
Add a "bad year" line to your cash flow: what income you expect if the main risk hits, and how you will still pay loans, school fees and inputs, for example from savings, a second enterprise or insurance. If you use crop or livestock insurance, check the insurer is licensed (in Kenya with the Insurance Regulatory Authority) and read the payout trigger.
You can ask a phone AI assistant to turn your notes into a neat table or to ask you questions about gaps in your plan, but the numbers must come from your own records and local prices. Do not type in ID numbers, account numbers or PINs.
Step by step:
- Copy your risk table from Lesson 1: top three risks.
- Add your two or three costed investments.
- Write how you will pay and your lender questions.
- Add two money-saving mitigation practices.
- Write your carbon offer rules.
- Add a bad-year cash-flow line and a review date.
Words to know:
- Business plan: a short written plan of what your farm does, its costs, income and goals.
- Bad-year scenario: a plan for what happens to income and payments if the main risk strikes.
- Payout trigger: the event, such as low rainfall measured at a station, that makes an insurance policy pay.
Official sources:
- Insurance Regulatory Authority, Kenya (check an insurer is licensed)
- FAO: Climate-Smart Agriculture Sourcebook
Try it now: Final task: write your one-page climate-resilience plan with all six parts and a bad-year cash-flow line. Read it to a family member, group member or extension officer and ask them for one question you have not answered.
You can now write a one-page climate-resilience plan for your farm business that a lender, buyer or programme can read.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Climate risks in money Risks are listed without likelihood or cost, or fewer than three. Three risks, each with likelihood and an estimated cost in local currency. Also shows business effects (loans, buyers, labour) and where the estimates came from. Costed investments Investments are named but not costed. Two or three investments with full cost, average yearly benefit and payback. Uses real local quotes and explains the choice of which to start first. Finance and lender checks No plan for paying, or a lender with no checks. Says how it will be paid and lists questions on total cost, repayment dates, conditions and licensing. Has compared two finance options and checked the lender on the regulator's list. Practices that save money No mitigation practice, or one with no saving shown. Two practices that cut emissions, each with the input or money saved. Includes payback for any practice that needs spending, such as a biodigester. Carbon offer rules No rules, or would sign or pay on the day. At least four checks: registry, payment and share, rights over land and trees, no fees, advice before signing. Names the national rules or office to check, such as Kenya's Carbon Markets Regulations. Complete one-page plan Parts are missing or there is no review date. All six parts, a bad-year cash-flow line and a review date on one page. Has been read by a group member, extension officer or adviser and updated with their question. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part of the plan and try again.

check.q: Which part is MISSING from this plan: risks, costed investments, how to pay, mitigation practices, carbon rules?
options: The farmer's favourite crop
A list of neighbours
The weather for tomorrow
A review date
check.why: A plan needs a review date so it is updated after each season.

check.q: What does a bad-year line in your cash flow show?
options: How much you will earn in the best year
How you will still pay loans and costs if the main risk hits
The price of fertilizer last year
How many workers you know
check.why: It tests whether the business survives the shock you rated most likely and costly.
